scientificFindings: PMMA repeat unit [–CH2–C(CH3)(COOCH3)–]n and MMA CH2=C(CH3)–C(=O)–O–CH3 are chemically compatible. Appropriate PMMA depolymerisation is a valid monomer-recovery example. Mechanical recycling largely preserves chains; purified MMA requires repolymerisation before comparison with usable PMMA granulate. No PE-to-ethene promise, hydrolysis requirement, or complete recovery claim is imposed.

Case A correctly compares equal independently stipulated functional quality and the same usable output: 40/80=0.50 kWh/kg; 120/80=1.50 EUR/kg; 100/75=1.333... kWh/kg; 225/75=3.00 EUR/kg. The 80 kg MMA intermediate is correctly not the 75 kg polymer denominator. 20/25 kg outside target product are recognised without claiming their ultimate fate.

Case B has a real changed-quality transfer, not numerical relabelling: 60 kg finished blend requires 45 kg regranulate and 15 kg virgin PMMA, hence 50 kg waste at 90% yield. Energy 18+45+6=69 kWh and cost 45+30+12=87 EUR. Monomer route needs 60/0.85=70.588... kg waste, 60 kWh, 90 EUR. Mechanical saves 3 EUR; monomer route saves 9 kWh. Blend strength is supplied test data and is not incorrectly interpolated.

Environmental judgement remains conditional on equal functional demand and disclosed boundaries. Operating energy is not complete environmental impact; missing emissions/energy carrier, auxiliaries, transport and residue data prohibit the universal greenest claim. Original didactic values are explicitly separated from measured plant data.

The official KCGO original physical/printed page 43 explicitly lists monomer recovery, thermoplastic remelting and ecological/economic aspects at common GK/LK level. The goal covers that common comparison without importing the separate LK hydrolysis/PE-cycle rows.

DE and EN have the same mechanism, quantities, boundaries, tasks and permissible conditional choices. The goal is one assessable comparative route judgement: explaining chain behaviour and normalising product data are supporting steps, not independent disconnected goals.

Actual native physical page 3 shows full current title, ID, image, description, external prerequisite and successors without clipping. The source image correctly contrasts retained symbolic chains with separate MMA then polymerisation, residual streams and conditional quality/yield/energy/cost comparison. This is an orientation aid, not measurement or source evidence.

scientificFindings: The central performance is one coherent supervised solubility/crystallisation investigation: control solvent mass and temperature, obtain own endpoint intervals, plot normalised saturation capacity, and explain the observed or absent crystallisation through that capacity. Distinguishing saturation from relative concentration is necessary to interpret this same investigation, not an unrelated second routine.

Case A supplied endpoints normalise by factor 20 to 31–33,45–47,63–65 g/100g water, midpoint 32/46/64. A 3.00g sample in 5.00g water is soluble at model 40°C capacity 3.20g; at 20°C capacity 1.60g leaves 1.40g equilibrium crystals, interval 1.35–1.45g. Local stipulated interpolation at 35°C gives 55g/100g water, 2.75g dissolved and 0.25g crystals. These values are model balances, not observed dry yields.

A 60g/100g water solution at 40°C is unsaturated relative to 64 yet more concentrated than a saturated 32g/100g water solution at 20°C. With 10.00g water, 20°C capacity is 3.20g, so all 3.00g stays dissolved with 0.20g additional capacity. A clear cooled 3g/5g sample can be supersaturated; clarity alone cannot certify unsaturation or realised crystals.

Case B correctly separates near-flat NaCl solubility from solvent-loss effects: ±0.05g endpoint in 5g water gives ±1.0g/100g water, larger than the 0.6 model change over 20–40°C. C: 1.80g capacity, 1.70g dissolved, zero crystals, 0.10g remaining. E after loss of exactly 1g water: 1.44g dissolved, 0.26g crystals, total mass 5.70g. The total loading 42.5g/100g water is not the dissolved concentration 36.0.

F contains 10g/100g water versus C34; both remain unsaturated. Supplied decreasing-S(T) substance R has capacity 1g at 40°C and 2g at 20°C: cooling leaves all 1g dissolved, 1g remaining capacity and no equilibrium crystals. This refutes a universal cooling rule without asserting a measured real-substance property.

Protocol explicitly requires authorisation, supervision, local safety assessment, small quantities and controlled baths, with oxidiser separation for KNO3. It checks weighing, time, temperature, endpoint persistence/repetition and solvent losses. Non-observation and delayed nucleation are allowed; fixed wait time and a lid do not prove equilibrium or zero loss. Wet crystals are not equated to dry solute yield.

Original G9 source physical page 13 / printed page 12 puts this exact row under Fakultative Unterrichtsinhalte/Aufgaben and includes saturation/concentration, graphs and crystallisation experiments. The source optional status is preserved; adopting this target does not make the source row universally compulsory.

DE/EN quantities, control conditions and tasks match. The original material cases are E1/G1 design evidence; no real execution, student understanding, practical success or human trial has been observed. A later actual supervised investigation plus substantive changed transfer can provide sufficient learner evidence within one sequence. Neither two whole practical cases nor a fabricated two-attempt quota is required.

Actual native physical page 4 shows the full current page without clipping.
